stages.title: Reactor physics
stages.hook: A reactor must keep a steady number of fissions for years. What does it mean for neutrons to be in balance?
explain: Reactor physics follows the neutron population. In each generation, some neutrons cause fission, some are absorbed without fission, and some leak out of the core. The multiplication factor k is the number of neutrons in one generation divided by the number in the one before.

If k is less than 1, each generation is smaller and the chain reaction dies away (subcritical). If k equals 1, the population is steady (critical), which is the normal state for a power reactor. If k is greater than 1, the population grows (supercritical), which operators allow only briefly and slowly when raising power.

Control is possible mainly because a small fraction of fission neutrons, less than one percent, are delayed: they come from fission products a few seconds after the fission. These delayed neutrons slow down changes in the chain reaction so that control rods and automatic systems have time to respond.

Reactors are also designed with negative feedback: if power or temperature rises, physical effects such as lower moderation or more neutron absorption reduce the reaction rate, which helps stabilise the reactor.

example.q: A generation has 1000 neutrons. If k = 0.9, how many neutrons are in the third generation after it?

analogies.farm: A herd where births and deaths balance stays the same size; if births exceed deaths it grows.
analogies.city: A bank account with deposits equal to withdrawals stays constant.
analogies.sport: A rally that continues at the same pace, as long as each shot is returned.
analogies.tech: A thermostat with feedback keeps temperature steady.

stages.mnemonic: k below one: dies; k at one: steady; k above one: grows.
terms: Neutrons in one generation divided by the previous generation.
The chain reaction is exactly self-sustaining (k = 1).
Neutrons released seconds after fission, making control easier.
A change that tends to reduce the cause of the change.

misc.wrong: 'Critical' means the reactor is in danger.
misc.right: In reactor physics, critical simply means the chain reaction is steady. A power reactor operates normally while critical.

stages.limits: This is a simplified, conceptual view. Real design uses detailed computer calculations and many safety margins.

panel.q: List three fates of a neutron in a reactor core and say which ones keep the chain reaction going.
panel.model: A neutron can cause fission (which keeps the chain going), be absorbed without fission (lost), or leak out of the core (lost). Only fission sustains the chain reaction.

teach.model: The multiplication factor k compares the neutrons in one generation with the previous one. If k is less than 1 the reaction dies away, if it is exactly 1 it is steady, and if it is greater than 1 it grows. Power reactors run at k = 1, and control rods and negative feedback keep it there.

stages.title: Nuclear reaction cross-sections
stages.hook: A neutron is fired at a thin foil. How can we measure how likely it is to hit a nucleus we cannot see?
explain: The cross-section σ measures how likely a particular reaction is between a neutron and a nucleus. Think of it as an effective target area: a larger area means a higher chance of interaction. It is measured in barns, where 1 barn = 10⁻²⁸ m².

Different reactions have different cross-sections: scattering, capture and fission. The cross-section also depends strongly on the neutron's energy. For fission in uranium-235, the cross-section for slow (thermal) neutrons is much larger than for fast neutrons. That is why moderators are used.

In a material with N nuclei per cubic metre, the macroscopic cross-section is Σ = N × σ, measured per metre. The average distance a neutron travels before an interaction, the mean free path, is 1 ÷ Σ.
The reaction rate per unit volume is Σ × φ, where φ is the neutron flux (how many neutrons pass per square metre per second). This is how engineers link the neutron population to power.

example.q: A material has N = 4 × 10²⁸ nuclei per m³ and σ = 0.5 barn (0.5 × 10⁻²⁸ m²). What is the mean free path?

analogies.sport: A bigger goal is easier to hit: the cross-section is the size of the goal.
analogies.city: A wider doorway is easier to walk through.
analogies.nature: A big target is easier for a rain drop to fall on.
analogies.tech: A radar sees a big aircraft more easily than a small one.

stages.mnemonic: Bigger barn, bigger chance. Σ = Nσ, path = 1/Σ.
terms: Effective target area for a reaction, in barns.
N × σ, the interaction probability per metre of travel.
Neutrons crossing unit area per second.

misc.wrong: The cross-section is the physical size of the nucleus.
misc.right: It is an effective area describing probability, and it varies with neutron energy and reaction type.

stages.limits: Real cross-sections have sharp resonances and are taken from measured data tables.

panel.q: Why can the same nucleus act as a good absorber of slow neutrons and a poor one of fast neutrons?
panel.model: Cross-sections depend on neutron energy. A slow neutron spends longer near a nucleus and many nuclei have much larger capture cross-sections at low energies, so the same nucleus can absorb slow neutrons far more readily.
panel.why: Energy dependence is a central feature of cross-sections.

A higher Σ
A higher density only

teach.model: A cross-section is the effective target area a nucleus presents to a neutron for a given reaction. A bigger cross-section means a higher chance of reaction. Multiply it by the number of nuclei per cubic metre to get the chance per metre, and the mean free path is the inverse. Cross-sections change with neutron energy.

stages.title: Reactor thermal hydraulics
stages.hook: Pumps push water through a core. How much flow is needed to carry away a given amount of power?
explain: Thermal hydraulics is the study of heat transfer and fluid flow. In a reactor, heat made in the fuel passes through the fuel pellet, the cladding, and into the coolant by conduction and convection. The coolant carries it away.

For steady flow, the heat carried is P = ṁ × c × ΔT, where ṁ is the mass flow rate (kg/s), c is the specific heat capacity and ΔT is the rise in coolant temperature across the core. For a given power, more flow means a smaller temperature rise.

Engineers must keep the fuel and cladding below limits. A key concern is boiling: if too much of the surface is covered by vapour, heat transfer drops sharply and cladding temperature can climb quickly. This is why designs keep a safety margin from this boiling limit.
Natural circulation lets hot, less dense fluid rise and cooler, denser fluid sink, moving heat even with no pump. Some designs rely on this to provide passive safety.

example.q: Coolant flows at 200 kg/s and warms by 30 °C passing through the core. Use c = 4200 J/kg°C. What power does it carry away?

analogies.home: A central-heating system: a pump moves hot water to radiators.
analogies.city: A river carrying away warm water from a factory.
analogies.sport: A runner with a fan blowing cool air over them.

stages.mnemonic: Power = flow × heat capacity × temperature rise.

misc.wrong: More coolant flow always means higher temperatures somewhere.
misc.right: For a fixed power, more flow gives a smaller temperature rise in the coolant, which usually helps.

stages.limits: Real flows are three-dimensional and need detailed computer models; this is a one-line energy balance.

stages.title: Nuclear materials
stages.hook: Inside a reactor, metals face heat, pressure, corrosion and a constant shower of neutrons. What would you build with?
explain: Materials in a reactor are chosen for several properties at once: strength at high temperature, resistance to corrosion, how strongly they absorb neutrons, and how well they withstand radiation damage.

Fuel cladding is often a zirconium alloy because zirconium absorbs few neutrons, so it wastes few of them, while being strong enough and corrosion resistant in hot water. The reactor pressure vessel is made of thick steel to contain high pressure.

Radiation damages materials. Fast neutrons knock atoms out of place in a metal and, over many years, can make steel more brittle (radiation embrittlement). Engineers include test samples in reactors and monitor them to check the vessel stays tough.

Other materials have specific jobs: boron and cadmium to absorb neutrons, graphite or water as moderators, and concrete for shielding. Zirconium can react with steam at very high temperatures to make hydrogen, which designers and safety systems must account for.

example.q: Why choose a zirconium alloy rather than ordinary steel for cladding inside the core?
steps: Cladding sits where neutrons are plentiful.
Zirconium absorbs far fewer neutrons than steel.
So fewer neutrons are wasted and the chain reaction is more efficient.
example.a: It absorbs few neutrons while remaining strong and corrosion resistant

analogies.city: A bridge uses materials checked regularly for fatigue.

stages.limits: Material choices vary by reactor type, and research continues on new alloys and ceramics.

stages.title: Radiation dosimetry
stages.hook: Two people each absorb the same energy from radiation, but one is hit by alpha particles and the other by gamma rays. Are the risks equal?
explain: Absorbed dose is the energy deposited per kilogram of tissue, measured in grays: 1 Gy = 1 J/kg. It tells us how much energy was absorbed, not how harmful it is.

Equivalent dose in sieverts (Sv) multiplies the absorbed dose by a radiation weighting factor wR to account for the biological effect of the type of radiation. wR is 1 for gamma rays, X-rays and beta particles, and 20 for alpha particles.

Effective dose adds up the equivalent doses to different organs, each weighted by a tissue weighting factor wT, to estimate the overall risk to the whole body. For example, wT is 0.12 for the lung and 0.04 for the thyroid.

Everyone receives natural background radiation, on average about 2.4 mSv per year worldwide, with large variation. Typical international guidance sets a public limit of 1 mSv per year above background and a worker limit averaging 20 mSv per year over five years.

example.q: A tissue absorbs 5 mGy of alpha radiation (wR = 20). What is the equivalent dose?

analogies.sport: A football and a bowling ball moving at the same speed have different impacts; energy alone does not tell the effect.
analogies.home: Same calories from different foods do not have the same nutrition.
analogies.city: Two noises with the same loudness can be more annoying if sharp.
analogies.nature: Equal sunlight energy does different harm to different skin.

stages.mnemonic: Gray = energy per kilogram; Sievert = Gray × weighting for harm.
terms: Absorbed dose × radiation weighting factor, in sieverts.
Sum of tissue-weighted equivalent doses for the whole body.

misc.wrong: A sievert and a gray are the same thing with different names.
misc.right: Both are joules per kilogram, but the sievert includes weighting for the effect of the radiation type and tissue.

stages.limits: Dose limits and risk estimates, such as from the linear no-threshold model for low doses, are based on assumptions that scientists continue to debate.

stages.title: Reactor instrumentation
stages.hook: A control room has hundreds of readings. What if one sensor gives a wrong value? How can operators trust the picture?
explain: Instrumentation and control (I&C) systems measure the state of the plant and act on it. Key measurements include neutron flux (power level), coolant temperature and pressure, water level, flow rate and radiation levels.

Neutron detectors placed in or near the core measure the neutron flux, which is proportional to fission power. Thermocouples and resistance thermometers measure temperature. Pressure and level sensors monitor the coolant system.

To avoid relying on a single sensor, safety measurements are redundant: several sensors measure the same quantity. A voting scheme such as two-out-of-three decides if action is needed: if any two of three sensors read a trip value, the system triggers. This protects against both a failed sensor missing a real problem and a faulty sensor causing a false alarm.

Automatic protection systems can insert control rods rapidly (a scram or trip) without waiting for an operator. Diverse systems based on different principles guard against a common fault affecting all of them. Control rooms are designed using human-factors research so operators can see clearly what is happening.

example.q: Three level sensors read: normal, low, low. With 2-out-of-3 voting, does the system trip?
steps: Count sensors showing the trip condition: 2.
Two meet the rule, so yes.

analogies.sport: Three referees: a decision needs two to agree.
analogies.home: Three smoke alarms: you act if two sound.
analogies.city: Three traffic cameras confirming an accident.
analogies.tech: Spacecraft computers often vote on results.

stages.mnemonic: Measure, vote, act: redundancy, diversity, independence.
terms: Having more than one component do the same job.

A device that measures neutron levels, linked to power.

misc.wrong: Adding more identical sensors always makes a system safer.
misc.right: Identical sensors can fail together from a common cause. Diversity and independence reduce that risk.

stages.limits: More complex systems may also add new ways to fail, so designers balance simplicity and redundancy.

questions.q: A software update is applied to all three redundant channels at the same time and has a hidden bug. What risk does this show?
o: Common-cause failure
Improved diversity between the channels
Lower cost for the whole system
No risk, as three copies are always safe

panel.q: Why do safety systems usually act automatically, at least at first?
o: Some events develop faster than humans can respond
Operators are not needed at all in a modern plant
Automation never fails, so no human check is ever required
It saves the plant money on the wages of its staff
panel.why: Automatic action covers fast events, with humans overseeing.

panel.q: What is the difference between redundancy and diversity? Give one example of each.
panel.model: Redundancy means having several copies of a component, like three identical sensors. Diversity means using different designs or principles for the same job, like a temperature sensor and a pressure sensor both signalling a problem.

panel.q: Operators are encouraged to report near-misses in I&C. How does this help?
o: It reveals weaknesses before they cause harm
It lets managers blame the staff involved
It hides faults so the plant looks safe
It slows the plant down in daily use

teach.model: Sensors measure power, temperature, pressure, level and radiation. Safety measurements use several sensors and a voting rule such as two-out-of-three, so one failure does not cause a miss or a false trip. If limits are crossed, an automatic scram inserts the control rods.

stages.title: Reactor safety systems
stages.hook: Imagine the worst day for a reactor: the grid fails and a pipe breaks. Which systems should keep people safe?
explain: Reactor safety rests on three basic functions: control the reactivity (the chain reaction), cool the fuel, and contain radioactive material. Each function has several systems to carry it out.

Reactivity control: control rods inserted by a scram, and in some designs a second, independent way such as injecting a neutron absorber into the coolant. Cooling: pumps, emergency core cooling systems with their own water supply, backup power generators and heat removal after shutdown. Containment: fuel cladding, the primary coolant boundary, and the containment building with filters and sprays in some designs.

Safety systems follow the principles of redundancy, diversity, independence and, wherever possible, passive operation, which needs no power or operator action. Engineers analyse design-basis accidents, such as a coolant pipe break or a loss of power, to show the plant stays within safety limits.

Lessons from accidents have driven improvements. Following the 2011 Fukushima Daiichi accident, which began with an earthquake and tsunami and the loss of power and cooling, many plants added extra backup power, flood protection and portable equipment, and ran new safety reviews.

example.q: A plant loses grid power. Name the systems that keep the fuel cooled.
steps: The reactor trips and control rods insert.
Emergency diesel generators or batteries supply power to pumps.
Passive systems may also provide cooling with no power at all.
example.a: Backup generators, batteries and passive cooling systems

analogies.home: A house with a smoke alarm, sprinkler, fire door and escape plan.
analogies.city: A hospital's backup generator takes over when the grid fails.
analogies.sea: A ship's lifeboats, bulkheads and alarms.
analogies.sport: A climber with a rope, a partner and a helmet.

stages.mnemonic: Control, Cool, Contain: the three Cs.
terms: Systems that supply water to the core after a loss of coolant.
Operation without power or operator action.
An accident the plant is designed to withstand.

misc.wrong: Safety systems only switch the reactor off.
misc.right: Switching off is just the first step. Cooling and containment must continue afterwards.

stages.limits: Beyond-design-basis events are rarer and harder to analyse. Plants use probabilistic assessment and extra measures to address them.

trip.prompt: Find the safety functions and list a system for each.

questions.q: Which are the three basic safety functions of a reactor?
o: Control reactivity, cool the fuel, contain radioactivity
Boil the water, spin the turbine and generate power for the grid
Mine the ore, enrich the uranium and ship the fuel
Make heat, make light and make sound in the core

questions.q: What does passive safety mean?
o: It works without power or operator action
It is slow and takes a long time to act
It is always shown on a screen in the control room
It needs extra pumps to work properly
questions.why: Gravity, natural circulation or stored energy drives it.

questions.q: Why must cooling continue after a scram?
o: Decay heat continues
The chain reaction restarts
Rods overheat
Water is cold
questions.why: Radioactive fission products still produce heat.

questions.q: A plant has 4 independent emergency cooling trains and needs at least 2 to work in an accident. If 1 is out for maintenance, how many remaining could fail while still leaving 2?

Order a typical response to a loss of coolant accident.
items: Sensors detect low pressure or level

questions.q: Explain why safety systems are made independent of each other.
questions.model: If systems share parts or depend on each other, one cause could disable them all. Independent systems mean that if one fails, the others can still do their job.

questions.q: After Fukushima, many plants added...
o: More backup power, flood protection and portable equipment
More fuel stored in a heap beside every reactor
Fewer inspections, to save the operators' time
Taller chimneys at the top of the main building
questions.why: Lessons learned led to extra layers.

questions.q: A plant is built on the coast. Which is a sensible design response to flood risk?
o: Site important backup equipment above the expected flood level
Ignore floods completely, since they are very rare in practice
Remove the outer walls so that any water can flow straight through

questions.q: A designer replaces a pump-driven cooling system with a gravity-fed tank. What benefit might result?
o: It works even with total loss of power
It is much stronger than any pump
It makes extra neutrons for the core
It raises the power of the reactor

panel.q: Why do engineers analyse events beyond the design basis even though they are very unlikely?
o: To find weaknesses and add margin
To scare the public about the plant
Because it is easy and costs nothing to do
To lower the power of the reactor

panel.q: A claim says 'the reactor was safe because the control rods were inserted'. Explain why that is incomplete.
panel.model: Inserting rods stops the chain reaction, but decay heat continues, so cooling must still work, and containment must keep radioactive material in. Safety needs all three functions.

panel.q: Which attitude supports safety culture most?
o: Questioning assumptions and reporting concerns without blame
Assuming that nothing can ever go wrong in a well-built plant
Hiding small errors so that the record always looks clean
Relying on one very strong barrier and nothing more
panel.why: A questioning attitude is part of safety culture.

teach.model: Safety rests on three functions: control the reactivity, cool the fuel, and contain radioactive material. Each has several redundant, independent and diverse systems, and passive designs that need no power. After a shutdown the fuel still makes decay heat, so cooling must continue.

stages.title: Nuclear fuel lifecycle
stages.hook: Uranium starts in the ground and ends up in a reactor. What journey does it take, and what happens afterwards?
explain: The front end of the fuel cycle prepares fuel. Uranium is mined and milled into a concentrate, converted to a form suitable for processing, and for most reactor types its fissile uranium-235 fraction is raised above the natural level (called enrichment). It is then fabricated into ceramic pellets inside metal fuel rods and assembled for loading.

In the reactor, fuel is used for several years. Fission uses up some uranium-235 and also converts some uranium-238 into plutonium, which can itself fission and supply part of the energy. Fission products build up and absorb neutrons, so after a time fuel is removed even though most of the uranium is still there.

The back end deals with used fuel. It is first cooled in pools, then stored. Some countries reprocess it, chemically separating uranium and plutonium for reuse in new fuel, which reduces the volume of high-level waste. Others dispose of it directly in a repository (an open or once-through cycle). Both approaches are debated.
Each stage has environmental, safety, security and economic issues, from mine tailings to transport safety, so regulation covers the whole cycle.

example.q: Order the front-end steps: fabrication, mining, enrichment, conversion.
steps: Then it is converted, enriched and finally fabricated into fuel.

analogies.farm: Grain: grown, harvested, milled, baked, eaten, and leftovers composted.
analogies.city: A recycling plant that sorts and reuses materials.
analogies.sea: A fishing fleet: catch, process, pack, sell.

stages.mnemonic: Mine, mill, convert, enrich, fabricate, burn, cool, then recycle or store.
terms: Raising the fraction of uranium-235 above natural levels for most reactor fuel.
Making fuel pellets, rods and assemblies.
Chemical separation of used fuel to recover uranium and plutonium.
Used fuel is stored and disposed of without reprocessing.
Everything from removing fuel to final disposal.

misc.wrong: Used fuel is just useless waste with no energy left.
misc.right: Used fuel still contains usable uranium and plutonium, which is why some countries reprocess it, though costs and security make this debated.

stages.limits: Different countries choose different strategies, and views differ on economics, security and waste policy.

Used fuel is stored in a pool and later pushed into the reactor again
Fuel is never stored anywhere and is simply left in the core
Fuel is burnt in a furnace like coal

questions.q: Why is fuel removed even though much uranium remains?
o: Fission products absorb neutrons and fuel performance falls
It melts inside the core after the first few months of use

questions.q: A reactor loads 90 tonnes of fuel and replaces one third each year. How many tonnes are replaced per year?

Match each stage to its purpose.

questions.model: For: it recovers uranium and plutonium for reuse and reduces the volume of high-level waste. Against: it is costly and complex, and separated plutonium needs strict security.

questions.q: A country with little uranium of its own considers reprocessing. Which factor might favour it?
o: Making more use of imported uranium
It removes all radioactivity from the fuel

questions.q: Why is the whole fuel cycle regulated and not just the power plant?
o: Mining, transport, storage and disposal all have safety and security issues
Only the reactors matter for safety and security, so the rest is left alone
The aim is to slow down the whole nuclear industry on purpose
The aim is to raise costs for the operators

panel.q: Why does the choice between open and closed cycles involve ethics as well as engineering?
o: It affects waste burden, security and costs for future generations
It is only a technical choice with no ethical side to it
Ethics is irrelevant to any engineering choice made today
It changes the laws of physics that govern the fuel

panel.q: Describe one environmental or social impact at the front end of the fuel cycle and how it might be managed.
panel.model: Uranium mining can leave tailings and affect water, land and local communities. Impacts are managed through regulation, monitoring, protection of workers, restoration of sites and consultation with the people affected.
panel.why: All parts of the cycle matter.

panel.q: Which is a fair statement?
o: No fuel cycle route is free of trade-offs
One route is perfect and has no drawbacks at all
Waste is only produced when fuel is reprocessed
Mining uranium has no effect on the land
panel.why: Each route has costs and benefits.

teach.model: Uranium is mined, processed into fuel and used in a reactor for several years. The used fuel is cooled in pools, then stored. Some countries reprocess it to recover material, and others dispose of it directly. Every stage is regulated for safety and security.

stages.title: Nuclear regulation and safeguards
stages.hook: Who checks the people who run nuclear plants, and how does the world make sure nuclear material is only used peacefully?
explain: National regulators license and inspect nuclear facilities. A good regulator is independent of the companies it oversees and of the bodies that promote nuclear power. It reviews designs, inspects construction and operation, can require changes or stop operations, and enforces the law.

International cooperation helps share good practice. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), founded in 1957, promotes safe and peaceful uses and provides safety standards and peer reviews. Countries are also bound by conventions on nuclear safety and on the management of radioactive waste.

Safeguards are measures to verify that nuclear material is not diverted from peaceful use. They include material accounting, inspections, seals and surveillance cameras. They are linked to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, which entered into force in 1970. Alongside this, security protects facilities and materials against theft and sabotage.

Professional ethics matter too. Engineers and operators must put safety first, be honest in reporting, respect the law and the public's right to information, and speak up about concerns. Societies debate nuclear energy openly, and decisions should rest on evidence and public participation.

example.q: A company reports a small safety issue to the regulator immediately, even though it is embarrassing. Which value is this showing?
steps: Reporting early helps the regulator and other plants learn.
This is open, honest safety culture and professional ethics.
example.a: Honest reporting and a strong safety culture

analogies.sport: Referees are independent of the teams so decisions are fair.
analogies.city: Building inspectors approve plans and check the work.
analogies.farm: Food inspectors check farms and markets.

stages.mnemonic: Independent regulators, international standards, inspections, honesty.
terms: An independent authority that licenses and inspects.
Verification that nuclear material stays in peaceful use.
Putting safety first in values and habits.

misc.wrong: Safeguards and safety are the same thing.
misc.right: Safety protects people from accidents and radiation. Safeguards verify that nuclear material is used only for peaceful purposes. Security guards against theft and sabotage.

stages.limits: Rules differ among countries, and opinions differ on how strict and how transparent regulation should be.

The power to award a prize to the operator

questions.model: People living near facilities and future generations are affected, so involving them builds trust, brings in local knowledge and respects their right to information and a say in decisions.

questions.q: Order a typical licensing path.
questions.why: Oversight continues throughout the plant's life.

Say nothing, since it is not their job

To compete with each other over who has the best safety scores

To lower the standards used in each country

panel.q: Why is 'regulatory capture' (a regulator becoming too close to industry) a worry?

It improves the regulator's independence
It lowers costs for everyone involved

panel.q: Present two different viewpoints on how much nuclear energy a country should use, and say what evidence would help decide.
panel.model: Supporters stress low-carbon, reliable electricity and energy security. Critics stress waste, accident risk, high costs and alternatives such as renewables. Evidence on costs, emissions, safety records, waste plans and reliability, combined with public discussion, can help decide.

panel.q: A statement says 'safety rules are enough, so we do not need an open culture'. What is wrong with it?

teach.model: Independent regulators license and inspect nuclear facilities. The IAEA helps with international standards, and safeguards such as accounting and inspections verify that nuclear material stays in peaceful use. Safety, security and safeguards are different, and honest reporting and public participation matter.
